Des policiers sont-ils nécessaires dans: Are police officers necessary in schools to prevent gun violence?

Le projet Équipe-école suscite des crain: The Équipe-école project is raising concerns among community organizations. Illustration: Nia E-K
<strong>La journée du 11 novembre a été: November 11 was marked by yet another incident involving weapons, this time in Laval, near Collège Montmorency. Three people were shot and injured, and the school remained closed until 10 p.m.
<strong>Ce drame est le dernier en date: This tragedy is the latest in a long series of shootings in the Montréal area this year. In response to this gun violence, authorities have announced, among other measures, the creation of an intervention team for Montréal schools: the Équipe-école. La Converse took a closer look at this initiative.
Quartier Saint-Michel, 16 h le 7 octobre: Saint-Michel neighbourhood, 4 p.m. on October 7. In the gym of a high school, about twenty young people are busy on the soccer field. Whistles blow; La Converse slips in to ask the teenagers there about the multidisciplinary school intervention team, better known as the Équipe-école.
Annoncée en septembre dernier par la Vil: Announced last September by the City of Montréal and the Service de police de la Ville de Montréal (SPVM), the initiative aims to create a team of police officers and professionals to prevent gun violence in the neighbourhoods affected by the phenomenon.
Sur le terrain de sport, les jeunes se s: On the sports field, the young people have gathered at their coach’s request. We ask them whether they have heard about this new structure, whose members will intervene in high schools. The answer is simple: nobody knows what it is. We would later find the same lack of awareness of the project among the 20 other young people we interviewed.
Ces rencontres ont toutefois suscité che: These conversations nevertheless raised questions among the teenagers about how the Équipe-école project works and how it was designed. Parents are asking these same questions, as are community organizers and an education professional we spoke with on the subject.
Le rôle de l’Équipe-école est d’agir « c: The role of the Équipe-école is to act “as a hub between schools, neighbourhood police stations and various institutional and community players,” says the SPVM. The municipal police force intends to “provide greater support to specialized workers,” notably through prevention activities. To support this new structure, Quebec’s Ministry of Public Security will invest more than $4 million over the next three years. The City of Montréal is contributing $400,000.
L’Équipe-école sera composée de 11 membr: The Équipe-école will be made up of 11 members: 5 uniformed police officers and 6 professionals from civil society. Among the latter will be three community development advisors. At the request of school administrations, officers will intervene in high schools with young people who display violent or at-risk behaviour. The officers will not, however, be based in the schools.
Alain Vaillancourt, responsable de la sé: Alain Vaillancourt, who is responsible for public security on the City of Montréal’s executive committee, says the Équipe-école’s interventions could, for example, include awareness-raising activities for parents and teachers on issues such as social media.
La police dans les écoles, ce n’est pas: Police in schools is nothing new. In the late 1980s, the Sûreté du Québec created the role of “police officer working in schools.” Today, students are familiar with “community social officers.” They work in elementary and high schools to, among other things, give presentations on bullying, sexual violence and violence prevention. Their role also includes identifying young people who are likely to be involved in criminal activity.
Le projet Équipe-école, qui doit débuter: The Équipe-école project, which is set to begin in mid-December, will also rely on a framework created in 1999 and updated in 2013, titled “Police Presence in Educational Institutions.”
« Quand j’étais à l’école secondaire, il: “When I was in high school, there was a lot of violence, and some of my friends ended up in the hospital because of problems they had at school,” says Anis, 20, a coach of a youth soccer team in Saint-Michel. “So if it’s possible to have more people there, that would be good,” he concludes.
« Le simple fait d’avoir la police dans: “Just having police in schools will keep students from fighting,” says a teenager sitting on a football field.
Marwa, étudiante en 2e année de cégep à: Marwa, a second-year CEGEP student in Hochelaga, also thinks the project could help reduce delinquency among young people.
Certains élèves ont en revanche exprimé: Some students, on the other hand, expressed reservations about the project. “If you’re close to the police, people will call you a snitch (informer, traitor, Editor’s note); you have to be careful, because nobody will want to have anything to do with you,” one high school student tells us.
Amadou, 15 ans, estime quant à lui que l: Amadou, 15, believes that the mere presence of police officers in a school could disturb students. “It’s not that you’re scared, it’s just that nobody likes it – it’s disturbing. Sometimes we’re there with friends, arguing, teasing each other for no reason; we’re goofing around, it’s nothing serious. They’re going to think we’re fighting,” he explains. Then he offers another argument: “Let me give you an example: you’re in a car, driving, and nobody likes driving with a police car behind them, following them. It doesn’t matter whether you’re doing something right or wrong.”
D’autres étudiants notent que la présenc: Other students note that police presence in schools is already common and doubt the approach’s effectiveness. “When I was in high school in Saint-Léonard, we often saw police officers in the hallways with the school workers; they were always close by,” says Kader, a CEGEP student.
«Moi, dans mon école, il y avait des age: “In my school, there were security guards,” says another CEGEP student, “but it didn’t reduce the violence. The students who wanted to fight went to the pizzeria outside the school.”
Plusieurs des jeunes issus de minorités: Several of the young people from visible minorities we spoke with also pointed out that, in their eyes, police in schools do not make them feel safer. “For us, when the police come to our schools, it’s not to talk,” says one of them.
La Ville de Montréal indique avoir consu: The City of Montréal says it consulted more than twenty young people last March to gather their views on fighting gun violence. The connection with these young people was made through community organizations.
Cette consultation s’est tenue dans le c: The consultation took place during a videoconference that lasted only two hours. Abdellah Azzouz is one of the 27 young people who took part in the working session. “I think the City should have done more work on the ground and not only gone through community organizations,” he says. “It would be better to go ask questions of a young person who hasn’t necessarily prepared to answer questions and who will say what they really think.” He feels the number of young people consulted is too small, but acknowledges that the City of Montréal made an effort to consult youth.
Cette question de la représentativité de: This question of how representative the young people met by the City were came up repeatedly in our conversations with high school and CEGEP students. One college student, for example, fears that teenagers show restraint or partly censor themselves when speaking with the institution. In his view, a meeting of this kind is not neutral. The young people, mostly from marginalized or stigmatized communities, might lack spontaneity in their answers or might factor into their interactions the preconceived ideas people may have about them.
Par ailleurs, une coalition d’organismes: Meanwhile, a coalition of community organizations denounced the project at a press conference on September 29. “We are very concerned about the spirit of the project, the way it was designed and the impact it will have on our young people and our families,” said Slim Hammami, coordinator of the Café-Jeunesse Multiculturel in Montréal-Nord. He laments that the community sector and parents were not consulted or informed about the project, and worries that young people from disadvantaged neighbourhoods will be further stigmatized by it.
Jacques Langlois, parent et président du: Jacques Langlois, a parent and the chair of the governing board of the high school his child attends, views the Équipe-école project favourably. “As a parent, I want the police to protect students,” he says. He also wants the SPVM to strengthen its relationship with his daughter’s school. In his eyes, the Équipe-école project therefore represents an “opportunity” for schools and police services to combat the rise in violence in schools.
Il souhaite en revanche que les étudiant: He does want school administrations to consult students before the Équipe-école program is rolled out. “It’s essential to know students’ limits. We need to know what they want and what they don’t want to ensure the project’s success,” concludes the father.
Aux abords de l’école Louis-Joseph-Papin: Outside the école Louis-Joseph-Papineau, all the parents interviewed by La Converse said they were reassured by the Équipe-école project. They believe the initiative “will deter a lot of violence in the surrounding area and in schools.”
La présence de policiers dans les écoles: Police presence in schools has a very long history. Illustration: Nia E-K
Rhoda Nanre Nafziger, assistante-profess: Rhoda Nanre Nafziger, an assistant professor at McGill University and a member of the École Sans Police collective, understands these parents’ concerns.
Elle juge toutefois que faire appel aux: She believes, however, that calling on law enforcement is not always an appropriate response to the problem of violence in educational institutions. “As Black parents, we internalize some of the negative views expressed about us. We tell our children, ‘Don’t be mean,’ but we don’t ask the system that hurts them to put an end to that suffering. We blame the child. But we need to understand that no matter what the child does, the system doesn’t change,”
Elle craint qu’une hausse de la présence: She fears that increased police presence in schools will have the opposite effect and ultimately increase the number of students who are incarcerated – what is known as the “school to prison pipeline.” This concept, developed in the United States, denounces a system that criminalizes students and sends them into the prison system after minor offences committed at school. Rhoda Nanre Nafziger also fears that the Équipe-école program will “target, above all, communities that are already marginalized and young people who may be at risk of dropping out.”
Interrogée à ce sujet, la Ville de Montr: Asked about this, the City of Montréal says the Équipe-école will not reproduce the biases observed in the United States.
Marlihan Lopez est une autre membre du c: Marlihan Lopez is another member of the École Sans Police collective, an offshoot of the Defund the Police Coalition. The organization was created following the killings of George Floyd and Breonna Taylor in the United States, and of Chantel Moore and Regis Korchinski-Paquet in Canada.
Marlihan Lopez estime qu’il est essentie: Marlihan Lopez believes it is essential to step up anti-bullying awareness efforts in schools. She argues, however, that this work is more a job for community organizations than for the police. In her view, these services can no longer be adequately provided because of the budget cuts successive provincial governments have inflicted on the community sector.
« [Le gouvernement et la Ville] disent q: “[The government and the City] say they have no money to raise teachers’ salaries or to have more resources in schools, but the City of Montréal is opening a community development advisor position for the Équipe-école project that pays around $68,000 to $108,000,” she observes.
Marlihan Lopez considère que la Ville de: Marlihan Lopez believes the City of Montréal has paid little attention to the views of those most affected: “It’s not the first time, in fact it’s always the same thing. [The City and the police] don’t consult and then they come along with these programs and projects,” she laments.
Elle juge primordial que les écoles obti: She considers it essential that schools receive more funding, and that young people have better access to extracurricular activities, psychologists, psychoeducators and teachers who are better trained in their realities.
Stéphanie, une enseignante du secondaire: Stéphanie, a high school teacher who prefers not to give her name, agrees. “Teachers who go to work in Montréal need to be better prepared about the communities there. Because teaching in Montréal is not the same as teaching in the regions. There are details that are important to know,” she says. She suggests that the training offered to future teachers include more information on Montréal’s cultural diversity.
Elle met également l’accent sur la créat: She also emphasizes building strong ties between parents and the school. “Without parents’ consent and involvement, the school alone won’t be able to do all the work,” she says. Then she adds: “People have the impression that the police are a magic solution. But do you want your child to avoid a behaviour because they’re afraid to do it, or do you want your child to avoid it because they don’t want to do it?” she asks.
Les 27 jeunes interrogés par la Ville on: The 27 young people consulted by the City also suggested possible solutions, which are presented in a report titled Perspectives sur les violences armées : le regard des jeunes. Among other things, they propose involving young people and their parents in the search for solutions, and increasing mental health resources for young people.
Interrogé au sujet de la démarche de con: Asked about the consultation process initiated by the City, Alain Vaillancourt says “it is difficult to consult everyone.” He says he spoke at length with residents and organizations that had concerns in order to ease their apprehensions by clarifying certain aspects of the project. He adds that, through street outreach workers, he met young people who do not go to community organizations.
Le service de communication du SPVM préc: The SPVM’s communications department, for its part, offers the following clarification: “The police officers who will visit the designated schools will be liaison officers, that is, specialized prevention officers. They will work jointly with the three civilian community development advisors who will be hired, but also in close collaboration with the socio-community officers at the neighbourhood police stations (PDQ), with the support of the SPVM’s civilian community development advisors already present in some PDQs across the territory.”
<em>*Nous avons interrogé des représenta: *We asked SPVM representatives about the Équipe-école initiative. Among other things, we asked which programs they had drawn inspiration from. The municipal police force mentioned initiatives in place in Glasgow, Toronto, New York and Boston. It should be noted that the City of Toronto ended its police program in public high schools in 2017. Since 2017, the Toronto public school board has in fact decided to remove the uniformed police program from 45 public schools. The initiative had been launched in 2008 following the death of Jordan Manners, 15, who was killed in the cafeteria of his high school. The program was removed from schools following a consultation of 15,000 students, 500 parents and 100 school staff members.
